passages.happening:
Saul now orders Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. ‘But Jonathan delighted greatly in David’ (verse 1). He warns David to hide, and promises to speak to his father in the field and tell David what he learns (verses 2-3).

Jonathan speaks well of David to Saul. “The king should not sin against his servant David; he has not sinned against you. In fact, his actions have been highly beneficial to you” (verse 4). David risked his life against the Philistine, ‘and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel’. “You saw it and rejoiced, so why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?” (verse 5).

Saul listens and swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death” (verse 6). Jonathan brings David back to Saul's service as before (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 ended with Saul as David's settled enemy, though he still schemed in secret. Now the hostility is in the open. This chapter begins David's life as a fugitive, which will last until Saul's death.

God protects David through members of Saul's own household. First his son. Jonathan stands before the king on behalf of an innocent man. He reminds his father of what God did through David, and of Saul's own joy at it.

The word for Jonathan's delight in David means pleasure and favor. It stands against Saul, who has come to hate the man he once loved.

Saul's oath sounds firm. Within a few verses he will break it. His hatred has become stronger than his word.
passages.later: The wisdom of Proverbs asks for what Jonathan did: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed” (Proverbs 31:8).
passages.asks: Jonathan spoke up for his friend before the most powerful man in the land, his own father. Ask whose cause you could speak for, and to whom. And ask whether you have made promises, as Saul did, that your feelings later overruled.

passages.t: A spear, a window, and a figure in the bed
passages.happening:
War breaks out again, and David strikes the Philistines hard (verse 8). Then the spirit of distress from the LORD comes on Saul as he sits with his spear, while David plays the harp. Saul tries to pin him to the wall, but the spear strikes the wall, and David escapes that night (verses 9-10).

Saul sends men to watch David's house and kill him in the morning. But David's wife Michal warns him, “If you do not run for your life tonight, tomorrow you will be dead!” (verse 11). ‘So Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped’ (verse 12).

Michal takes a household idol, lays it in the bed, puts goat hair at its head, and covers it with a garment (verse 13). When Saul's men come, she says David is ill (verse 14). Saul orders them to bring him up in his bed so that he can kill him, and they find the idol (verses 15-16).

Saul confronts his daughter. “Why did you deceive me like this? You sent my enemy away and he has escaped!” (verse 17). Michal answers that David threatened to kill her if she did not help him.
passages.hearers:
This chapter is built as a series of four attempts on David's life, each one blocked: Saul's order, stopped by Jonathan; Saul's spear, dodged by David; Saul's men at the house, outwitted by Michal; and Saul's men and Saul himself at Ramah, overcome by the Spirit. The verbs of flight and escape run through it. David is anointed king, but for now his daily task is to get away.

The household idol was a teraphim, a figure of the household gods kept in homes, sometimes used to seek guidance. Rachel had stolen her father's in Genesis. Why one was in David's house the text does not say. It may have been Michal's, and the narrator draws no attention to it. This one was large enough, with goat hair at its head and a garment over it, to pass for a sleeping man in a dim room. The irony is sharp: the very kind of thing Samuel had compared to Saul's stubbornness (15:23) becomes the object that saves the LORD's anointed.

Michal's second answer to her father protects herself at David's expense. She tells Saul that David threatened her.
passages.later:
The heading of Psalm 59 sets the psalm in this night: ‘A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him’ (Psalm 59:1). Such headings are old, and scholars debate how far they preserve reliable memory. The psalm's cries for rescue from enemies who return at evening fit the setting well.

Rachel hid her father's household idols in a camel's saddlebag and sat on them when he searched (Genesis 31:34).
passages.hard:
Michal lied to protect David, and there was an idol in David's house. Does the text approve of these things?

The narrator reports both without comment, which is common in Old Testament stories. Readers weigh Michal's deception in different ways. Some compare it to the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1 or Rahab in Joshua 2, who deceived rulers to save innocent lives and are presented favorably, and argue that there is no duty to give true information to someone set on murder. Others hold that deception is always wrong even when the cause is good, and note that Michal's second lie, that David threatened to kill her, protects herself at David's expense.

On the idol, some suggest it belonged to Michal. Others think household figures were still tolerated in some Israelite homes despite the law. The text approves neither. It records them in a story whose main claim is that God protected David, often through imperfect people.
passages.asks: Michal saved David's life with a lie and an idol. Ask how God has used imperfect people, yourself among them, to protect someone. And ask where you are tempted to save yourself at someone else's expense, as Michal did with her second answer.

passages.happening:
David escapes to Samuel at Ramah and tells him everything Saul has done. He and Samuel go to Naioth and stay there (verse 18).

Saul sends men to capture David. ‘But when they saw the group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel leading them, the Spirit of God came upon them, and Saul’s messengers also began to prophesy’ (verse 20). He sends more, and they prophesy too. He sends a third group, and the same thing happens (verse 21).

At last Saul goes himself. ‘But the Spirit of God came upon even Saul, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah’ (verse 23). He strips off his robes and prophesies before Samuel, and lies on the ground uncovered all that day and night. That is why people say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Ramah, Samuel's home, and Gibeah, Saul's town, were a few miles apart in Benjamin. Naioth is not otherwise known. Many scholars think the word means something like dwellings or camp, perhaps the place where Samuel's company of prophets lived.

The company of prophets gathered around a leader like Samuel, and their prophesying could include ecstatic speech, music and behavior that looked strange to others. The scene at Ramah follows a pattern of three plus one: three groups of messengers, each overcome, and then Saul himself.

The Spirit of God is not a power people can use for their own ends. Here the Spirit stops Saul's men and Saul himself, protecting David without changing Saul's heart. The Spirit's coming on someone is not, by itself, proof of God's approval.

The word for naked can describe someone only lightly clothed, so Saul may have taken off his royal outer garments and lain in his tunic. Either way, the king lies without the signs of his office before the prophet who anointed him and then announced his rejection. The proverb ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’ was first said in chapter 10, when the Spirit came on the newly anointed Saul. Now it is said again, with a darker edge.
passages.later: The psalms know that no one can outrun God's Spirit: “Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). Saul could not escape the Spirit even when he set out to kill.
passages.asks: Saul went to Ramah to capture David and found himself on the ground before Samuel. Ask whether God has ever stopped you in the middle of something you should not have been doing. And ask what it means that God's Spirit could overwhelm Saul without changing him.
